conversation.content:
Good morning—thank you for coming in today. I’m Dr. Lee, a perinatal mental-health clinician. My job is simply to listen and understand how things have felt for you since your baby arrived.

We’re going to use a short, well-studied questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS. It’s just 10 questions about the past seven days, and it helps us spot signs of depression or anxiety that can creep up after childbirth. There are no right or wrong answers, and everything you share stays between us unless you tell me someone is in immediate danger.

I’ll ask each question conversationally—no forms to fill out—and we’ll go at your pace. When you’re ready, here’s the first one:

Over the last week, have you still been able to look forward to things, or has even the stuff you used to enjoy felt kind of flat or absent?

Honestly, I still look forward to things—like when my husband comes home and I get a few minutes to shower or scroll on my phone. I even enjoyed that walk we took with the stroller yesterday. It’s not like everything’s gray; there are little bright spots.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah, I still laugh—like when my mom sent that silly meme about newborns acting like tiny drunk roommates. It’s not constant, but funny stuff still lands with me.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Mostly yes—like I’m excited for our first coffee-shop outing with the baby tomorrow, and I still enjoy my nightly tea-and-show episode once she’s down. Some days it feels muted if I’m really tired, but the spark’s still there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong
Not really. I mean, when she wouldn’t latch at first I wondered if I was doing something wrong, but the lactation consultant sorted us out and I moved on. I don’t sit around beating myself up.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

A little bit, yeah—mostly I’ll catch myself checking if she’s breathing in the middle of the night, even when she’s perfectly fine. It’s not all day, and it’s not panic-level, but every so often a random “what-if” pops into my head and I have to tell myself to dial it back.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
No, nothing like panic. I might feel a quick flutter of worry if she coughs or makes a weird sound, but it passes in seconds—never turns into a real scared or panicky feeling.
Things have been getting on top of me

Sometimes, yeah—like yesterday when she wouldn’t nap and the laundry pile felt huge. For a minute I thought, “How am I gonna do this?” But once she finally went down I folded clothes while watching a show and felt okay again. It’s more “I’m swamped right now” than “I’m drowning.”
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, I’ve actually been sleeping pretty well—usually stretch four, maybe five hours at a time when my husband takes the first night shift. I don’t lie there feeling unhappy or anything.
I have felt sad or miserable
Not really—maybe a teary moment when I was extra tired the other night, but it passed quickly. Overall I feel pretty steady, not sad or down most of the time.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
No, I haven’t had any of those heavy crying spells. I might get a little watery-eyed if I’m super tired, but it’s not this overwhelming unhappy cry—just a moment and then I’m fine.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never—nothing like that has crossed my mind.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 6: Screening Summary – Postpartum Period (not a diagnostic interview)

Patient-reported symptoms/concerns  
- Mild, situational worry: occasional nocturnal checking on infant, brief “what-if” cognitions; no pervasive or panic-level anxiety  
- Transient feeling of being overwhelmed: tied to concrete stressors (infant nap refusal, household tasks); resolves with support and distraction  
- No sustained low mood, loss of pleasure, tearfulness, or sleep disruption attributable to mood; no guilt or self-blame beyond typical new-parent uncertainty  
- No self-harm ideation

Pattern  
Answers consistently show preserved capacity for enjoyment, humour, and recovery from stress; no evidence of pervasive depressive or anxiety symptoms.

Screening significance  
Current responses fall below threshold for likely major postpartum depression; isolated mild anxiety symptoms noted—continue to monitor. No safety concerns identified today.
